prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I hear America singing, the varied carols I hear, Those of mechanics, each one singing his as it should be blithe and strong, The carpenter singing his as he measures his plank or beam, The mason singing his as he makes ready for work, or leaves off work, The boatman singing what belongs to him in his boat, the deckhand singing on the steamboat deck, The shoemaker singing as he sits on his bench, the hatter singing as he stands, The wood-cutter’s song, the ploughboy’s on his way in the morning, or at noon intermission or at sundown, The delicious singing of the mother, or of the young wife at work, or of the girl sewing or washing, Each singing what belongs to him or her and to none else, The day what belongs to the day—at night the party of young fellows, robust, friendly, Singing with open mouths their strong melodious songs.

outputs.L3:
The poem celebrates the many different voices of working Americans and presents them as part of one larger national song. Instead of focusing on a single speaker or one type of person, it highlights a wide range of workers, suggesting that America is made up of many individual lives, occupations, and experiences. Together, these voices create a collective expression of the nation’s identity.

Each worker sings while carrying out their own trade, which shows a sense of pride, dignity, and individuality in labor. The mechanic, carpenter, mason, boatman, and others are not portrayed as anonymous workers, but as people whose work has meaning and value. Their songs reflect their personal connection to what they do, suggesting that labor is not only necessary but also a source of self-expression and strength.

The poem also includes both men and women, which broadens its vision of American life. By recognizing women’s work, including domestic labor, the poem gives importance to tasks that might otherwise be overlooked. This inclusion shows that the nation is shaped not only by public trades and visible professions, but also by private, household work and everyday responsibilities.

A key idea in the poem is that every person’s song is unique. Each song belongs specifically to the worker who sings it, just as each person’s life and labor are their own. This emphasis on individuality suggests that people contribute to America in different ways, and that these differences should be valued rather than erased.

Overall, the poem presents America as energetic, joyful, strong, and united. Its unity does not come from everyone being the same, but from many distinct voices singing together. Through this image of a nation made up of diverse workers and songs, the poem celebrates both individual freedom and collective identity.
outputs.L4:
Walt Whitman’s poem “I Hear America Singing” explores American identity through the lives and labor of ordinary workers. Instead of describing the nation through political leaders, famous events, or grand institutions, Whitman presents America as a collection of working people, each engaged in a daily task. The carpenter, mason, boatman, shoemaker, wood-cutter, mother, young wife, and others all appear as part of a broad national portrait. Their “songs” are not necessarily literal music, but expressions of energy, pride, skill, and individuality. Each person contributes to the life of the country through honest work, and each voice has its own distinct sound.

The poem’s catalog structure emphasizes variety. Whitman lists different kinds of laborers, showing that America is made up of many roles, trades, and experiences. No single worker represents the whole nation; rather, the nation is formed by the combination of all of them. The mechanic sings while working, the carpenter sings as he measures wood, the mason sings on his way to a job, and the boatman sings what belongs to him and his work. These details suggest that every kind of labor has dignity. Whitman treats physical work not as something lowly or invisible, but as a source of identity, creativity, and freedom.

At the same time, the poem finds unity in this diversity. Although each worker sings a separate song, together their voices create a shared democratic chorus. Whitman’s America is not uniform; it is strong because its people remain individual while still belonging to a larger whole. The repeated image of singing suggests joy, confidence, and participation. Each person has a place, and each person’s contribution matters. The nation becomes beautiful not because everyone is the same, but because many different voices can exist side by side.

The poem also reflects Whitman’s democratic ideals. By focusing on common workers, he celebrates the people who build, maintain, and sustain the country. He suggests that American greatness comes from everyday labor and from the pride individuals take in their work. The poem honors the independence of each person while also imagining a collective national harmony. In this way, “I Hear America Singing” presents America as a living chorus: diverse, energetic, hardworking, and united by the shared contributions of ordinary people.

Those who travel through the country often notice its variety: busy cities, quiet towns, wide deserts, tall mountains, and long coastlines. The culture of America is also diverse, influenced by many communities, traditions, and dreams. From music and food to literature and innovation, America continues to be a place where people seek opportunity, express identity, and imagine new possibilities.
